response.title: Waves — describing and measuring them
response.summary: A wave transfers energy without transferring matter, and everything measurable about one comes from two questions: which way does the oscillation point relative to the travel, and how do you put numbers on the shape. One page of your photographs could not be read, so this rebuilds what was legible and says plainly where the gap is.
objectives: Define wavelength, frequency, amplitude and phase difference.
Use the wave equation to relate speed, frequency and wavelength.

blocks.text: A wave carries energy, not matter. In a transverse wave the oscillation is perpendicular to the direction of travel; in a longitudinal wave it is parallel.

blocks.definition: The distance between two adjacent points in phase, measured in metres.
The number of complete waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz.
The maximum displacement from the equilibrium position, measured in metres. It is measured from the middle, not from trough to crest.

blocks.useWhen: You know two of speed, frequency and wavelength and want the third.

blocks.text: Intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude: doubling the amplitude gives four times the intensity. Intensity is measured in W m⁻² and amplitude in m, so this is a proportionality, not an equation you can evaluate without a constant.

blocks.caption: A transverse wave with amplitude and wavelength marked. The numbers are illustrative — they show the shape, not a measurement.
blocks.alt: A sine curve of displacement against distance, with the peak height labelled amplitude and the distance between successive equivalent points labelled one wavelength.

blocks.text: Phase difference is measured in radians, and 2π radians corresponds to one whole wavelength.

blocks.title: Converting a distance to a phase
blocks.text: Divide the path difference by the wavelength and multiply by 2π. Half a wavelength apart is π radians — exactly out of phase.

flashcards.back: The distance between two adjacent points in phase, in metres.
Complete waves passing a point per second, in hertz.
v = fλ, with v in m s⁻¹, f in Hz and λ in m.
From the equilibrium position to the maximum displacement, not trough to crest.

flashcards.front: Double the amplitude — what happens to intensity?
flashcards.back: It quadruples. Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared.

quiz.prompt: Sound is a longitudinal wave because:
choices: the oscillation is parallel to the travel
it cannot travel through a vacuum
quiz.answer: the oscillation is parallel to the travel
quiz.explanation: That is the definition. The vacuum point is true of sound but is not what makes it longitudinal.

quiz.prompt: A wave has frequency 250 Hz and wavelength 1.4 m. What is its speed?

quiz.answer: The distance between two adjacent points in phase.
quiz.explanation: Any two equivalent points work — crest to crest is the easiest to see.

quiz.prompt: The amplitude of a wave is tripled. The intensity is:
quiz.explanation: Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, and three squared is nine.

quiz.prompt: Two points on a wave are one quarter of a wavelength apart. What is their phase difference in radians?
quiz.explanation: A full wavelength is 2π, so a quarter of one is π/2.

quiz.prompt: Which quantity is measured in hertz?
quiz.explanation: Hertz is one per second, which is what a frequency counts.
